section.title: The Bread of Life
section.sectionRationale: The fourth and fifth signs, the feeding of the five thousand and the walking on water, set up the Gospel's first great I am discourse. Jesus refuses the crowd's bread-king enthusiasm and points them past perishing food to Himself, the true bread from heaven. The teaching that His flesh, given for the life of the world, must be eaten by faith proves so hard that many disciples turn back, leaving the Twelve, through Peter, to confess that He alone has the words of eternal life.
section.thesis: Jesus is the true bread from heaven, greater than the manna, who gives His flesh for the life of the world, so that everyone the Father gives Him and who comes and feeds on Him by faith has eternal life and will be raised at the last day, a teaching that sifts the crowd and reveals who truly believes.
section.frameNote: Five movements: the feeding of the five thousand; the walking on the water and the words It is I; the discourse on the true bread from heaven and I am the bread of life; the hard saying about eating His flesh and drinking His blood; and the sifting, as many turn back and Peter confesses the words of eternal life.

units.label: The feeding of the five thousand
units.note: the fourth sign, bread in the wilderness

verses.text: After this, Jesus crossed to the other side of the Sea of Galilee (that is, the Sea of Tiberias).
A large crowd followed Him because they saw the signs He was performing on the sick.
Then Jesus went up on the mountain and sat down with His disciples.
Now the Jewish Feast of the Passover was near.
When Jesus looked up and saw a large crowd coming toward Him, He said to Philip, “Where can we buy bread for these people to eat?”
But He was asking this to test him, for He knew what He was about to do.
Philip answered, “Two hundred denarii would not buy enough bread for each of them to have a small piece.”
One of His disciples, Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, said to Him,
“Here is a boy with five barley loaves and two small fish. But what difference will these make among so many?”
“Have the people sit down,” Jesus said. Now there was plenty of grass in that place, so the men sat down, about five thousand of them.
Then Jesus took the loaves and the fish, gave thanks, and distributed to those who were seated as much as they wanted.
And when everyone was full, He said to His disciples, “Gather the pieces that are left over, so that nothing will be wasted.”
So they collected them and filled twelve baskets with the pieces of the five barley loaves left over by those who had eaten.
When the people saw the sign that Jesus had performed, they began to say, “Truly this is the Prophet who is to come into the world.”
Then Jesus, realizing that they were about to come and make Him king by force, withdrew again to a mountain by Himself.

units.label: Jesus walks on water
units.note: It is I; do not be afraid

verses.text: When evening came, His disciples went down to the sea,
got into a boat, and started across the sea to Capernaum. It was already dark, and Jesus had not yet gone out to them.
A strong wind was blowing, and the sea grew agitated.
When they had rowed about three or four miles, they saw Jesus approaching the boat, walking on the sea, and they were terrified.
But Jesus spoke up: “It is I; do not be afraid.”
Then they were willing to take Him into the boat, and at once the boat reached the shore where they were heading.

units.label: The true bread from heaven
units.note: I am the bread of life

verses.text: The next day, the crowd that had remained on the other side of the sea realized that only one boat had been there, and that Jesus had not boarded it with His disciples, but they had gone away alone.
However, some boats from Tiberias landed near the place where the people had eaten the bread after the Lord had given thanks.
So when the crowd saw that neither Jesus nor His disciples were there, they got into the boats and went to Capernaum to look for Him.
When they found Him on the other side of the sea, they asked Him, “Rabbi, when did You get here?”
Jesus replied, “Truly, truly, I tell you, it is not because you saw these signs that you are looking for Me, but because you ate the loaves and had your fill.
Do not work for food that perishes, but for food that endures to {{zoe|eternal life}}, which the Son of Man will give you. For on Him God the Father has placed His seal of approval.”
Then they inquired, “What must we do to perform the works of God?”
Jesus replied, “The work of God is this: to believe in the One He has sent.”
So they asked Him, “What sign then will You perform, so that we may see it and believe You? What will You do?
Our fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, as it is written: ‘He gave them bread from heaven to eat.’”
Jesus said to them, “Truly, truly, I tell you, it was not Moses who gave you the bread from heaven, but it is My Father who gives you the true bread from heaven.
For the bread of God is He who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world.”
“Sir,” they said, “give us this bread at all times.”
Jesus answered, “{{egoeimi|I am}} the {{artos|bread of life}}. Whoever comes to Me will never hunger, and whoever believes in Me will never thirst.
But as I stated, you have seen Me and still you do not believe.
Everyone the Father gives Me will come to Me, and the one who comes to Me I will never drive away.
For I have come down from heaven, not to do My own will, but to do the will of Him who sent Me.
And this is the will of Him who sent Me, that I shall lose none of those He has given Me, but raise them up at the last day.
For it is My Father’s will that everyone who looks to the Son and believes in Him shall have eternal life, and I will raise him up at the last day.”

units.label: The bread is My flesh
units.note: given for the life of the world

verses.text: At this, the Jews began to grumble about Jesus because He had said, “I am the bread that came down from heaven.”
They were asking, “Is this not Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? How then can He say, ‘I have come down from heaven?’”
“Stop grumbling among yourselves,” Jesus replied.
“No one can come to Me unless the Father who sent Me draws him, and I will raise him up at the last day.
It is written in the Prophets: ‘And they will all be taught by God.’ Everyone who has heard the Father and learned from Him comes to Me,
not that anyone has seen the Father except the One who is from God; only He has seen the Father.
Truly, truly, I tell you, he who believes has eternal life.
I am the bread of life.
Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, yet they died.
This is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that anyone may eat of it and not die.
I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. And this bread, which I will give for the life of the world, is My {{sarx|flesh}}.”
At this, the Jews began to argue among themselves, “How can this man give us His flesh to eat?”
So Jesus said to them, “Truly, truly, I tell you, unless you eat the flesh and drink the blood of the Son of Man, you have no life in you.
Whoever eats My flesh and drinks My blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up at the last day.
For My flesh is real food, and My blood is real drink.
Whoever eats My flesh and drinks My blood {{meno|remains}} in Me, and I in him.
Just as the living Father sent Me and I live because of the Father, so also the one who feeds on Me will live because of Me.
This is the bread that came down from heaven. Unlike your fathers, who ate the manna and died, the one who eats this bread will live forever.”

units.label: Many turn back; Peter confesses
units.note: Lord, to whom would we go?

verses.text: Jesus said this while teaching in the synagogue in Capernaum.
On hearing it, many of His disciples said, “This is a difficult teaching. Who can accept it?”
Aware that His disciples were grumbling about this teaching, Jesus asked them, “Does this offend you?
Then what will happen if you see the Son of Man ascend to where He was before?
The Spirit gives life; the flesh profits nothing. The words I have spoken to you are spirit and they are life.
However, there are some of you who do not believe.” (For Jesus had known from the beginning which of them did not believe and who would betray Him.)
Then Jesus said, “This is why I told you that no one can come to Me unless the Father has granted it to him.”
From that time on many of His disciples turned back and no longer walked with Him.
So Jesus asked the Twelve, “Do you want to leave too?”
Simon Peter replied, “Lord, to whom would we go? You have the words of eternal life.
We believe and know that You are the Holy One of God.”
Jesus answered them, “Have I not chosen you, the Twelve? Yet one of you is a devil!”
He was speaking about Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot. For although Judas was one of the Twelve, he was later to betray Jesus.

egoeimi.gloss: I am. Here begins the great series of I am sayings in John, in which Jesus completes the phrase with an image, I am the bread of life. The words echo the divine name, I AM, revealed to Moses; on the sea Jesus uses the phrase absolutely, It is I, literally I am, do not be afraid. Each saying reveals who Jesus is and what He gives.

artos.gloss: Bread, food, the basic staple of life. Jesus takes the miracle of loaves and the memory of manna and declares Himself the true bread from heaven, the bread of God who gives life to the world. Physical bread sustains for a day and cannot conquer death; this bread, eaten by faith, gives life forever.

zoe.gloss: Life, especially eternal life, the life of God and of the age to come. In this chapter it is contrasted with food that perishes; the true bread endures to eternal life. To have this life is to be raised up at the last day, so that eternal life embraces both a present possession by faith and a future resurrection.

sarx.gloss: Flesh. The bread Jesus gives for the life of the world is His flesh, a plain pointer to His death on the cross, His body given up. To eat His flesh and drink His blood is to receive by faith the crucified Christ and all the benefits of His death. Jesus adds that the Spirit gives life and the flesh, understood in a merely physical way, profits nothing.

meno.gloss: To remain, abide, stay. Whoever feeds on Christ by faith remains in Him, and He in them, a mutual indwelling that will be unfolded fully in the vine and the branches. To abide is not a fleeting contact but a settled, living union with Christ from which life continually flows.

basic.context: Near Passover, Jesus feeds a crowd of five thousand from a boy's five loaves and two fish, with twelve baskets left over. The crowd wants to make Him king by force, so He withdraws, and that night He comes to the disciples walking on the sea, saying, It is I, do not be afraid. The next day the crowd finds Him, still hungry for more bread, and Jesus turns them from perishing food to Himself, the true bread from heaven. When He says the bread is His flesh, given for the world, and that they must eat it, many are offended and leave. Peter, for the Twelve, says, Lord, to whom would we go? You have the words of eternal life.
basic.hermeneutics: Jesus keeps moving people from the physical to the spiritual: from loaves to the bread of life, from manna to Himself. The key question is what it means to eat this bread, and Jesus answers plainly, whoever comes to Me and believes. Eating His flesh and drinking His blood is vivid language for receiving the crucified Christ by faith. This is a hard teaching that sifts the crowd; the chapter shows that true faith is a gift the Father gives, and that it clings to Christ even when the teaching is difficult.
basic.originalLanguages: The discourse turns on a few words. Jesus says ego eimi, I am, the bread of life, the first named I am saying. He is the true artos, the bread from heaven, greater than the manna. He gives His sarx, His flesh, for the life of the world, pointing to the cross. To feed on Him is to have zoe, eternal life, and to meno, to remain, in Him and He in us.
basic.typology: The manna in the wilderness, bread from heaven that could not conquer death, foreshadows the true bread, Christ, who gives life forever. The Passover setting points to the Lamb whose flesh is given for the world. The feeding on a mountain recalls God spreading a table for His people.
basic.christ: Christ is the true bread from heaven who comes down to give life to the world. He walks on the sea and speaks the divine It is I. He gives His flesh in death for the life of the world, and He keeps every one the Father gives Him, raising them at the last day. He alone has the words of eternal life.
basic.god: The Father gives the true bread, draws people to the Son, and grants them to come. His will is that the Son lose none but raise them at the last day. Salvation is His gracious initiative from beginning to end, even as it calls for real faith.
basic.crossReferences: Exodus 16 and Psalm 78 recount the manna. Isaiah 54 promises that all will be taught by God. Deuteronomy 8 says man does not live by bread alone. The Lord's Supper, in the other Gospels, echoes eating Christ's body and blood.
basic.oneStory: The God who fed Israel with manna now gives the true bread from heaven, His own Son, whose flesh is given for the life of the world. The Passover points to the Lamb, and the hard call to feed on Christ divides the crowd, gathering a people who, drawn by the Father, cling to the one who has the words of eternal life.

context.literary:
John 6 is the centre of a three part structure that the Gospel repeats. A sign is given, a discourse explains it, and the crowd divides. Here the two signs come first, the feeding of the five thousand, verses 1 to 15, and the walk on the sea, verses 16 to 21. The feeding is told in all four Gospels, and John alone adds the long conversation that unpacks it.

The conversation moves in a ladder of questions, each one lifting Jesus' meaning a step higher. The crowd asks when he arrived, verse 25, and he answers about their motives. They ask what to do, verse 28, and he answers 'believe.' They ask for a sign, verse 30, and he answers that the Father gives the true bread. They say 'give us this bread,' verse 34, and he answers 'I am.' The Jews grumble, verse 41, and then argue, verse 52, and each time Jesus does not soften what he has said but deepens it. At verse 51 the word shifts from believing to eating, and the language becomes as hard as it can be.

Two devices hold the discourse together. One is the refrain 'I will raise him up at the last day,' which appears in verses 39, 40, 44 and 54, so that every stage of the argument ends in resurrection. The other is the movement from the Father's giving, verses 32 to 40, to the Father's drawing, verses 41 to 51, to the Son's own flesh, verses 52 to 58.

Verses 59 to 71 are the aftermath and the real ending. The same crowd that wanted to make Jesus king, verse 15, is reduced to the Twelve, verse 67, and the chapter closes on the first mention of Judas, verses 70 and 71. Notice that the chapter is bracketed by two crowds and two mountains: in verse 3 Jesus goes up with his disciples, and in verse 15 he withdraws alone. The scene begins in abundance and ends in desertion, and Peter's confession is the only light left in the room.
context.historical:
The feeding falls near Passover, verse 4, in spring, which fits the detail that there was 'plenty of grass,' verse 10, and that the loaves were barley, the first grain to ripen. Barley was the bread of the poor. The numbers are carefully given. Philip's 'two hundred denarii' is a sum the BSB footnote explains as a labourer's pay for about two hundred days, Matthew 20:2, so the problem was out of reach by any ordinary means. John counts only the men, verse 10, 'about five thousand,' and Matthew 14:21 adds women and children.

The crowd's reaction is political. 'Truly this is the Prophet who is to come into the world,' verse 14, is Deuteronomy 18:15 spoken at the very moment bread appears in a lonely place, with echoes of the wilderness and the manna. A leader who could feed an army was just what a people under Roman rule hoped for, and verse 15 says they were about to 'make Him king by force.' Jesus refused a kingdom that was offered on those terms, and the refusal is the first cause of the chapter's later desertion. Some Jewish writings of the period or soon after expected that manna would fall again in the age to come, which helps explain why the crowd asks for a sign in terms of manna, verses 30 and 31.

The Sea of Galilee is called the Sea of Tiberias in verse 1, after the city Herod Antipas built on its shore, a name John uses only here and in 21:1. The disciples set out after dark and a strong wind rose, verses 17 and 18, as it still does on that lake when cold air drops from the hills. They had rowed about three or four miles by the BSB footnote's reckoning, which put them far out and in real danger.

The final scene is in the synagogue at Capernaum, verse 59, and the setting adds weight to the teaching. To a Jew, drinking blood was forbidden outright, Genesis 9:4 and Leviticus 17:10 to 14, since life was in the blood, Leviticus 17:11. Jesus' words in verses 53 to 56 would have sounded as shocking to his hearers as anything in the Gospels, which makes the hearers' reaction, 'This is a difficult teaching,' verse 60, quite understandable.
context.canonical:
The manna story in Exodus 16 is the backdrop for the whole discourse. God said, 'I will rain down bread from heaven for you,' Exodus 16:4, and Israel asked 'What is it?' because they did not know, Exodus 16:15. The crowd's quotation in verse 31 is marked by the BSB footnote as Psalm 78:24, with Exodus 16:4 also in view, and Nehemiah 9:15 gives the same memory: 'In their hunger You gave them bread from heaven.' Moses himself explained the purpose in Deuteronomy 8:3: God gave manna 'so that you might understand that man does not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD,' a text Jesus used in the wilderness, Matthew 4:4. John 6 deliberately returns to it.

Isaiah supplies the invitation. 'Why spend money on that which is not bread, and your labor on that which does not satisfy?' Isaiah 55:2, stands behind Jesus' command in verse 27 not to work for food that perishes. Isaiah 54:13, 'all your sons will be taught by the LORD,' is quoted in verse 45 to explain how the Father draws people.

In the later books the same imagery returns. At the Last Supper Jesus took bread and said, 'This is My body, given for you,' Luke 22:19, and Paul asks whether the bread we break is 'a participation in the body of Christ,' 1 Corinthians 10:16. Revelation promises 'hidden manna' to the one who overcomes, Revelation 2:17, and a multitude about whom it is said, 'Never again will they hunger, and never will they thirst,' Revelation 7:16, which fulfils verse 35. The words of verse 39, that none of those given to the Son will be lost, stand beside John 10:28 and 29 and John 17:12, and Peter's confession in verse 69 matches the cry of the demon in Mark 1:24, 'the Holy One of God,' but now spoken by a friend.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
John gives the discourse so that his readers will see what the feeding was for. The loaves were a sign, and a sign that is mistaken for the meal it points to has failed. Verse 26 is the key: the crowd followed because they were full, not because they understood. John writes for believers who were being tempted to leave, and for seekers who liked Jesus' kindness but not his claims. He wants both to see that faith in Jesus is not admiration for a wonder worker but a coming to him for life, which will cost them the right to make him into what they wanted.

John also means the chapter to show that unbelief is not the end of the matter. The Father gives, draws and teaches, verses 37, 44 and 45, so that no one who comes has done it unaided, and no one who comes will be cast out. This is meant as a comfort for believers in a hostile world. When many leave in verse 66 the reader is not to conclude that the cause has failed. It is meant to know that those the Father gives are kept, verse 39, and that to hold fast in a hard season is itself the work of God, verse 29.

Peter's answer in verses 68 and 69 voices the response John hopes his readers will make, as John 20:31 shows. 'To whom would we go? You have the words of eternal life.' The chapter ends with the question put to every reader: do you want to leave too?
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The two signs are descriptive. Nothing here tells believers to expect a miraculous feeding, or to walk on water, or to take Jesus' withdrawal from the crowd as a rule that Christians must refuse every public role. The detail that the disciples were afraid in a storm is a record of what happened, not a promise that storms will cease.

The teaching is where the chapter turns prescriptive. Do not labour for the food that perishes, verse 27, without forgetting that this does not forbid honest work, which Paul commands elsewhere. Believe in the one the Father has sent, verse 29. Come to Jesus, who will never turn you away, verse 37. The sentence about eating his flesh and drinking his blood is not a command to perform a particular ritual, since Jesus himself says 'the flesh profits nothing' and 'the words I have spoken to you are spirit and they are life,' verse 63. How far the Lord's Supper is in view is debated, but the heart of the instruction is to receive Christ himself, crucified for the world's life, and to go on feeding on him by faith.

The story of the departure in verse 66 describes a real pattern of what happens when Jesus' words are hard, and it is not a command to be hard on those who struggle. Jesus asks the Twelve, 'Do you want to leave too?' with no threat and no pressure, and Peter's answer is the model response.

debates.question: What does eating Jesus' flesh and drinking His blood mean?

views.label: Believing in the crucified Christ
views.case: Verses 35 and 47 equate coming and believing with the satisfaction Jesus describes with bread and drink, and verse 63 says 'the flesh profits nothing.' Augustine summed up this reading in the words 'Believe, and you have eaten.' Many Protestant interpreters, Calvin among them, hold that the chapter is about faith, and that the Lord's Supper is a sign and seal of the same feeding, not the primary subject here.

views.label: The Lord's Supper and the real presence
views.case: Roman Catholic teaching reads these verses as pointing to the Eucharist, where Christ gives himself under the signs of bread and wine, and notes that the Greek verb of verses 54 to 58 is a strong word for chewing, not a gentle one. Lutheran readers also find the Supper in view, though they differ about how. John does not record the Supper itself, and some think he put this discourse in its place as its interpretation.

views.label: Both, with faith as the means
views.case: Others hold that the discourse is about faith first, and that the Supper afterwards gives a visible form to the same reality, so that the sign and what it signifies belong together without being identical.

debates.bearing: All sides agree that Christ is received only by the believing reception of him, and that no one is saved by a rite apart from him. Whether the Supper is in view or not, the verse tells us what a believer must do: come hungry, and take what the Father has given.

debates.question: How do the Father's drawing and human coming fit together?

views.label: The Father's grace is decisive
views.case: The verb helko, 'draws,' in verse 44 is strong, and verse 65 says 'no one can come to Me unless the Father has granted it to him.' Everyone given to the Son will come, verse 37, and none will be lost, verse 39. On this reading the drawing is effective and personal, and is what makes the difference between those who come and those who do not.

views.label: The drawing is for all and may be resisted
views.case: In 12:32 Jesus says that when he is lifted up he will draw 'everyone' to himself, and the same word is used. On this view the Father's drawing is wide and genuine, and those who refuse do so against it. Verse 36, 'you have seen Me and still you do not believe,' shows a real offer refused.

views.label: Both statements are held side by side
views.case: The text says that the Father draws and that people must come, and John does not explain how the two fit. Verse 40 gives the human side: 'everyone who looks to the Son and believes in Him shall have eternal life.'

debates.bearing: The practical result is the same either way: no one who comes will be turned away, verse 37, and anyone who comes may take it as evidence that the Father has been at work. The gift of faith is not a reason for pride but for thanks.

debates.question: What does the departure in verse 66 show about those who leave?

views.label: They never truly belonged
views.case: Jesus says in verse 64 that some did not believe, and 1 John 2:19 says of those who left, 'if they had belonged to us, they would have remained with us.' The promise of verse 39 that none of those given will be lost is then kept intact.

views.label: Genuine believers can fall away
views.case: Others point to John 15:6, which warns that a branch that does not remain is thrown away, and to Hebrews 6:4 to 6, and read verse 66 as a warning that those who followed him can turn back.

views.label: They were disciples in a looser sense
views.case: The word 'disciples' in verses 60 and 66 includes the crowd of followers around the Twelve, and many of them had never moved beyond fascination with the signs, verse 26.

debates.bearing: The chapter wants its readers neither presumptuous nor anxious. It invites us to stay with Christ because he has the words of life, and promises that those who are the Father's gift are kept.

study.originalLanguages:
Look first at the verbs of eating. In verses 49 to 53 John uses the usual verb for eating, esthio. In verse 54, after the shock of verse 53, he switches to trogo, which in everyday Greek has the sense of munching or gnawing and is used of animals feeding. He keeps trogo for verses 56 to 58. The change is unlikely to be accidental: Jesus presses the point past the polite word, and the effect is to make the hearers face the physical reality of the incarnation and the cross.

The Father 'draws' people, verse 44, with the verb helko. It is a strong word, used elsewhere for dragging a net, John 21:6, or drawing a sword, John 18:10. It is also the verb of 12:32, 'I will draw everyone to Myself.' Verse 45 explains how the Father draws: 'they will all be taught by God,' a quotation of Isaiah 54:13, and the Greek there is didaktoi theou, 'God taught.' The drawing takes place through teaching, and the one who has heard and learned comes.

Verses 41, 43 and 61 use gongyzo, 'grumble.' The Greek translation of Exodus 16 uses the same verb family for Israel's grumbling against Moses and the LORD in the wilderness, so the crowd that quotes the manna story is behaving like the people in it. In verse 61 Jesus asks whether this teaching 'offends' them, from skandalizo, the verb that gives us scandal, meaning to cause someone to stumble. The disciples then 'turned back,' literally went away to the things behind, verse 66.

Verse 39 says Jesus will 'lose' none of those the Father has given. The verb is apollymi, which also means to perish. John 3:16 promises that believers will not 'perish,' and 10:28 says they 'will never perish.' The negative in verse 37, 'I will never drive away,' is the strong double negative ou me, used again in verse 35 for 'never hunger.' It is an emphatic denial, 'by no means.'

In verse 27 God has 'placed His seal of approval' on the Son. The verb, sphragizo, means to mark with a seal and so to authenticate. The Father has stamped the Son as genuine, so that he alone can give the food that lasts. Finally, in verse 11 Jesus 'gave thanks,' from eucharisteo, and the same verb appears in verse 23. It is the verb from which the word Eucharist comes, and the Last Supper accounts use it too, Luke 22:19. John does not describe the Supper, yet he chooses this verb twice.

typology.fulfillment: God rained down bread from heaven and Israel gathered it each morning, Exodus 16:4. It kept them alive in the wilderness, but its limits were plain: 'Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, yet they died,' verse 49. Christ is the bread that does what manna could not, giving life that death cannot undo, verse 58. The people had to gather manna each day, and Jesus teaches that his people feed on him continually, verse 56. Revelation 2:17 promises 'hidden manna' to the overcomer. The type falls short because manna fed the body and ended at the border of the land, while Christ feeds the whole person and does not end.

A man brought Elisha twenty barley loaves, and Elisha said to feed a hundred men, because the LORD said 'They will eat and have some left over,' and so it was. John's boy with five barley loaves, verse 9, and the leftover pieces, verse 13, are written to call this to mind, and the crowd's reaction in verse 14 shows they were thinking of a prophet. The escalation is great: twenty loaves for a hundred men becomes five loaves for five thousand, and the one who does it is not a prophet who speaks the LORD's word but the Word himself. The type falls short because Elisha was a servant who prayed for provision, while Jesus gives thanks and distributes as the Father's Son.

typology.type: The sea and the exodus, Psalm 77:19 and Job 9:8
typology.fulfillment: The LORD alone 'treads on the waves of the sea,' Job 9:8, and 'Your path led through the sea, Your way through the mighty waters,' Psalm 77:19. At the Red Sea he brought Israel through on dry ground, and Isaiah 43:2 promises his people, 'When you pass through the waters, I will be with you.' In verses 16 to 21 Jesus does what is said only of God, and says 'It is I; do not be afraid,' words that some hear as an echo of the divine self-revelation of Exodus 3:14, 'I AM WHO I AM.' The type falls short only in that the sea was crossed by Israel on the ground below, while here the Lord himself walks on the water, and the boat reaches shore at once.

The chapter's setting is Passover, verse 4. In Exodus 12 the people ate the lamb whose blood marked their doors, Exodus 12:7 and 8, and so were spared. Jesus now says that his flesh is to be given 'for the life of the world,' verse 51, and that the people must eat it and drink the blood, verses 53 and 54. John the Baptist had called him 'the Lamb of God,' John 1:29, and Paul says 'Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed,' 1 Corinthians 5:7. The type falls short because the lamb could protect one household for a night, while Christ's offering gives life to the world and does not need to be repeated.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ by contrast, with manna and with Moses. 'It was not Moses who gave you the bread from heaven, but it is My Father who gives you the true bread from heaven,' verse 32. The point is not to belittle Moses, but to say that the gift he mediated was a picture of one that comes in person. The Father gives the bread, and the bread is a person who 'comes down from heaven and gives life to the world,' verse 33. That makes the Son the real thing the Old Testament was reaching toward. Where Israel asked 'What is it?' of the manna, Exodus 16:15, John asks the reader 'Who is He?'

The chapter also leads to Christ by showing the shape of his death. He says the bread is his flesh, given 'for the life of the world,' verse 51. The word flesh points back to John 1:14, where the Word 'became flesh,' and forward to the cross. This is why the bread must be eaten and the blood drunk: the life that the Son offers is available only through his giving of himself. Paul says the same in 1 Corinthians 11:26: as often as we eat and drink we 'proclaim the Lord's death until He comes.' It is wise not to read more than the text gives, and the discourse itself says what the eating means, in verses 35 and 47, which is coming and believing.

Verses 20 and 62 show his glory. The Christ who comes to frightened men on the sea and says 'It is I; do not be afraid' is the one the Old Testament says walks on the waves. In verse 62 he asks what they will do if they 'see the Son of Man ascend to where He was before,' a reference to the resurrection and ascension that will answer their offence. The title 'Son of Man' appears in verses 27, 53 and 62, and it is as the Son of Man that he gives food, gives life and ascends.

Finally, the chapter shows the Christ who keeps those the Father gave him. 'I shall lose none of those He has given Me, but raise them up at the last day,' verse 39. He holds on to the Twelve even as one of them is a devil, verse 70, and in John 17:12 he says that none has been lost except the son of destruction. The pattern is a loving Lord whose grip does not depend on the strength of those he holds.
study.god:
The first thing the chapter shows about God is that He is the giver. The Father gives the bread, verse 32; gives the people to the Son, verse 37; and grants coming to those he will, verse 65. He 'sent' the Son and the living Father is the source of the Son's life, verse 57. At every stage of the salvation story in this chapter, the initiative lies with God. That keeps worship humble. We bring nothing to the table except hunger, and the invitation of Isaiah 55:1 and 2, 'come, buy, and eat ... without money and without cost,' is carried out in the one who is the bread.

Second, God is faithful to His purposes. The will of the Father is stated twice: 'that I shall lose none of those He has given Me,' verse 39, and that 'everyone who looks to the Son and believes in Him shall have eternal life,' verse 40. The Father's will is not a hope but a settled intention, and the Son carries it out. John 10:29 says 'No one can snatch them out of My Father's hand.' This is why the chapter can end in a desertion without losing its confidence: the people were never in doubt in the Father's mind, and Peter's answer is itself the Father's gift.

Third, God is the one who tests. Verse 6 says Jesus asked Philip where to buy bread 'to test him, for He knew what He was about to do.' The same God who tested Israel with manna, Exodus 16:4, tests his people through lack, and uses their helplessness to show his sufficiency. Deuteronomy 8:3 gives the reason: so that they would learn to live by every word that comes from his mouth.

Fourth, the chapter holds together things that are hard to hold. God is sovereign in drawing, and people are truly responsible for refusing. He is sovereign over the sea and yet present in the boat. He is the living Father who gives life to the Son, verse 57, and the Son who gives life to the world. The life of the Father and the Son is not poured out in distant space but is given in bread and flesh, a God who comes close enough to be eaten. Worship therefore takes the form of thanks, as the verb eucharisteo suggests, and of staying near: 'To whom would we go?' verse 68.

crossReferences.note: God promises to rain down bread from heaven and to test whether the people will follow His instructions. The crowd's quotation in verse 31 draws on this, and Jesus' reply in verse 32 corrects it: the giver was the Father, and the true bread is the one now before them.

The Israelites asked 'What is it?' for they did not know what it was, and Moses answered that it was the bread the LORD had given. Jesus' hearers likewise ask what he is, and the answer is that he is what the Father has given, though few see it.

God gave manna so that Israel would learn that man does not live on bread alone but on every word from the LORD's mouth. Verse 63 and Peter's 'You have the words of eternal life,' verse 68, carry that lesson to its end in the Son himself.

He rained down manna and gave grain from heaven, and man ate the bread of angels. The BSB footnote names this psalm as the source of the quotation in verse 31, which sets the crowd's request for a sign against a text that also tells of Israel's unbelief.

The LORD invites the thirsty to come and eat without money and asks why anyone would spend on what is not bread. Verse 27 and verse 35 read like an answer to this call, and the promise that those who listen will live in verse 3 matches the life of verse 40.

Verse 45 quotes this verse, that all will be taught by the LORD, and the BSB footnote confirms it. It explains the Father's drawing as teaching, and presents faith in Jesus as the fruit of the promised new covenant instruction.

Elisha fed a hundred men with twenty barley loaves and some was left over, as the LORD had said. The barley loaves, the question of how so little could feed so many, and the leftovers in John 6:9 and 13 all invite a comparison in which Jesus is greater.

The LORD alone treads on the waves of the sea. When the disciples see Jesus walking on the sea in verse 19 they are seeing what the Old Testament says only God does, and His words in verse 20 confirm it.

The life of the flesh is in the blood, which God has given on the altar to make atonement. This shows why the language of drinking blood in verse 53 is so shocking and so rich: the life offered is atoning life, given by sacrifice.

A close friend who shared the bread has lifted his heel against the speaker. Jesus applies this verse to Judas in John 13:18, and it throws a shadow on verse 71, where one who ate the bread was to betray him.

The bread we break is a participation in the body of Christ, and because there is one loaf the many are one body. Paul shows how the early church heard John 6: those who feed on Christ are bound to him and to each other.
Never again will they hunger, and never will they thirst. It carries the promise of verse 35 into the new creation, where those who came to Jesus find it fully kept.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a table. In Genesis 1 and 2 God gives food freely, and in Genesis 3 a meal taken in distrust brings death into the world. Almost every later story of food in Scripture takes place against that background: Israel hungry in the wilderness, the manna that was enough for each day, the prophets who feed a hundred on a few loaves, the feasts of the law, and the promise of a banquet to come. Hunger in the Bible is more than physical; it is the shape of human need, and the question running through the story is who can satisfy it.

John 6 answers by pointing to a person. The Father who once rained down manna now gives 'the true bread from heaven,' verse 32. The Passover setting, verse 4, places the answer inside the exodus story, where a lamb was eaten and the blood marked the door, and the answer in verses 51 to 58 gives the lamb a new meaning: his flesh is given 'for the life of the world.' The manna could not keep anyone from dying, verse 49. This bread can, verse 58, and so the chapter is the point where Israel's wilderness story reaches its goal.

What it sets up comes quickly. The Last Supper will turn the bread and cup into a sign of that death, Luke 22:19, and the church will go on keeping it 'until He comes,' 1 Corinthians 11:26. The cross is the place where the flesh is given, and the Spirit gives life, verse 63, a thought John takes up in the chapters that follow. Judas, named at the close of the chapter, brings the story back to the table where a friend who shared the bread lifts his heel, Psalm 41:9.

The story ends in the new creation with a fulfilment that mirrors the beginning. The tree of life stands beside the river, Revelation 22:2, and the multitude 'will never again hunger,' Revelation 7:16. The overcomer is given hidden manna, Revelation 2:17. Between the first meal and the last, the question for every reader is the one Jesus puts to the Twelve: 'Do you want to leave too?' Peter's answer is the whole story in a sentence: 'Lord, to whom would we go?'

quiz.q: What does Jesus want the crowd to seek after the feeding?

options.text: Not perishing food, but the food that endures to eternal life, which He gives.
options.note: Verse 27 redirects them from bread that perishes to the eternal food only He gives.

options.text: More bread to satisfy their hunger.
options.note: Jesus rebukes them precisely for coming because they ate their fill, verse 26.

options.text: A political king who would provide for their needs.
options.note: The crowd wanted to make Him king by force, but Jesus turns them from that to eternal food.

options.text: To believe in the One God has sent, the work of God.
options.note: True, and Jesus says this in verse 29, but the direct answer to what they should seek is the food that endures to eternal life.

quiz.q: What does Jesus mean by I am the bread of life?

options.text: He Himself is the true bread from heaven; those who come to Him and believe will never hunger and have eternal life.
options.note: Verse 35 defines the image: coming and believing satisfy forever and give life.

options.text: He provides literal bread whenever people are hungry.
options.note: The point is spiritual; He is the bread, received by faith, not a source of endless literal loaves.

options.text: He is greater than the manna Moses gave.
options.note: True, He surpasses the manna, but the fuller claim is that He Himself is the bread of life to be received by faith.

options.text: He offers wisdom and teaching that nourish the soul.
options.note: His words give life, but the claim is that He Himself, received by faith, is the life-giving bread.

quiz.q: What does eating Jesus' flesh and drinking His blood chiefly mean?

options.text: Receiving the crucified Christ by faith, so that He gives eternal life.
options.note: The discourse equates it with coming and believing, verses 35, 47, and 63.

options.text: A literal, cannibalistic consuming of His body.
options.note: Jesus says the Spirit gives life and the flesh profits nothing; the language is not literal cannibalism.

options.text: Sharing in His death and its benefits.
options.note: True and central, but it stops short of naming faith as the means by which we receive Him.

options.text: Merely admiring His sacrificial example.
options.note: It is far more than admiration; it is a living reception of Christ Himself by faith.

quiz.q: Why does Jesus say some do not come to Him even after seeing the signs?

options.text: Because no one can come unless the Father draws and grants it, and some do not believe.
options.note: Verses 44, 64, and 65 ground coming to Christ in the Father's gracious drawing.

options.text: Because the signs were not impressive enough.
options.note: The signs were clear; the issue is unbelief and the need for the Father's drawing.

options.text: Because they did not understand His teaching intellectually.
options.note: The deeper problem is unbelief and the lack of the Father's granting, not mere intellectual confusion.

options.text: Because faith is a gift that the Father must grant.
options.note: True, but it omits the paired reality that some simply did not believe, which the text also states.

quiz.q: How does Peter respond when many disciples turn back?

options.text: Lord, to whom would we go? You have the words of eternal life; we believe You are the Holy One of God.
options.note: Verses 68 and 69 record Peter's confession on behalf of the Twelve.

options.text: He quietly considers leaving as well.
options.note: The opposite; Peter confesses there is nowhere else to go but to Christ.

options.text: He affirms that Jesus has the words of eternal life.
options.note: True and central, but it leaves out his fuller confession that Jesus is the Holy One of God.

options.text: He insists the teaching was easy to accept.
options.note: The teaching was hard; Peter's point is not its ease but that Christ alone has the words of life.

questions: The crowd followed Jesus for bread that perishes. What perishing things do you find yourself seeking from Jesus, rather than seeking Him as the bread of life?
Jesus said whoever comes to Me I will never drive away. How does that promise meet you if you feel unworthy or unsure of your welcome?
Feeding on Christ means receiving Him by faith day by day. What would it look like this week to feed on Jesus rather than merely admire Him?
When the teaching got hard, many turned back, but Peter said, to whom would we go? Where is Jesus asking you to keep following even when His words are difficult?
The Father promises that the Son will lose none He is given and will raise them at the last day. How does that security change the way you face doubt and death?

translationNotes.note: Three or four miles renders the Greek measure; the BSB footnote gives about twenty-five or thirty stadia, roughly 2.87 to 3.45 miles. The detail underscores that they were far from shore when Jesus came walking on the sea.
He gave them bread from heaven to eat quotes Psalm 78:24 (see also Exodus 16:4), the manna tradition that frames the whole discourse.
They will all be taught by God quotes Isaiah 54:13, which Jesus links to the Father's drawing of people to Himself.
The Holy One of God; the BSB footnote records a variant in some manuscripts, You are the Christ, the Son of the living God. Either reading is a high confession of faith.
